Explain why a wrong classification misstates profit and asset values
Prepare the Trading Account of a sole proprietor and separate direct from indirect expenses

slides.narration: At the end of the year a sole proprietor turns the trial balance into financial statements. The Trading Account gives the gross profit, the Profit and Loss Account gives the net profit, and the Balance Sheet shows assets and liabilities. First, we learn to separate capital items from revenue items, because that decides what goes where. We work with an imagined firm, Farhan Textiles.

slides.heading: Capital expenditure
slides.body_md: **Capital expenditure** gives a benefit for more than one accounting year and acquires or improves a fixed asset.

rows: Lasts for more than one accounting year
To acquire a fixed asset, or to improve one so that it earns more or lasts longer
Non-recurring: it is not spent again every year
As an asset in the Balance Sheet
Land, machinery, furniture; carriage and fitting charges on a new machine; legal fees on buying a building

visual.alt: Table of the features of capital expenditure: benefit for more than one year, purpose of acquiring or improving a fixed asset, non-recurring, shown as an asset, with examples

slides.narration: Capital expenditure gives a benefit for more than one accounting year. It is spent to acquire a fixed asset, or to improve one so that it earns more or lasts longer. It is not repeated every year, and it appears as an asset in the balance sheet. Carriage and fitting charges on a new machine are part of its cost, so they are capital expenditure too.

slides.heading: Revenue expenditure
slides.body_md: **Revenue expenditure** is used up within the year, in running the business or maintaining the assets.

rows: Used up within the accounting year
To run the business or to maintain the assets in their working condition
Recurring: it is spent again every year
Charged to the Trading Account or the Profit and Loss Account
Wages, rent, salaries, repairs, electricity; carriage on goods bought for resale

visual.alt: Table of the features of revenue expenditure: benefit within the year, purpose of running the business or maintaining assets, recurring, charged to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account, with examples

slides.narration: Revenue expenditure gives its benefit within the accounting year. It is spent to run the business or to keep the assets in working condition, and it recurs every year. It is charged to the trading account or the profit and loss account. Wages, rent, repairs and electricity are examples, and so is carriage on goods bought for resale.

visual.caption: Capital and revenue expenditure compared.

slides.narration: Compare the two columns. Capital expenditure buys or improves a fixed asset, gives a benefit beyond the year and is shown as an asset. Revenue expenditure keeps the business running, is used up within the year and is charged against profit. Ask two questions about any payment. Does it create or improve an asset? Is its benefit longer than one year?

slides.heading: Quick check: classify the payment
slides.body_md: Decide the class of the fitting charges paid by an imagined printing press.
slides.narration: Think about what the payment achieves. Does it help get a fixed asset ready for use, or does it only keep something working? That decides whether the cost belongs with the asset or with the expenses of the year.

slides.heading: Receipts, and deferred revenue expenditure

rows: Money received that does not come from the normal trading of the year and that adds to capital or reduces an asset
Capital brought in by the proprietor; a loan received; sale of a fixed asset
Money received from the normal trading and incomes of the year
Sale of goods; commission, interest and rent received
A revenue expense whose benefit lasts for several years, so the part not yet charged is carried forward
A heavy advertising campaign for a new product

visual.alt: Table of capital receipts, revenue receipts and deferred revenue expenditure with meanings and examples

slides.narration: Receipts are classified in the same way. A capital receipt does not come from the trading of the year, for example capital brought in by the proprietor, a loan, or the sale of a fixed asset. A revenue receipt comes from trading and incomes, such as sales and commission. A heavy advertising campaign is a revenue item whose benefit lasts several years, so it is called deferred revenue expenditure.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classify the payments of Farhan Textiles
slides.body_md: **Farhan Textiles**, an imagined firm, made seven payments. Capital: **₹1,58,000**; revenue: **₹34,800**; deferred: **₹60,000**.
bullets: The loom, its carriage and its fixing are all capital.
Wages, oil and repainting are used up within the year.

rows: Cost of bringing the asset to its place
Cost of getting the asset ready
Oil and cleaning of the looms
Heavy launch advertising, benefit for three years

visual.alt: Classification of seven payments of Farhan Textiles: the loom, its carriage and its fixing, 1,58,000 rupees in all, are capital expenditure; wages, oil and cleaning, and repainting, 34,800 rupees in all, are revenue expenditure; the launch advertising of 60,000 rupees is deferred revenue expenditure

slides.narration: Farhan Textiles, an imagined firm, made seven payments. The loom, the carriage on it and the cost of fixing it are capital expenditure, which comes to rupees one lakh fifty eight thousand. Wages, oil and cleaning, and repainting are revenue expenditure, which comes to rupees thirty four thousand eight hundred. The launch advertising of rupees sixty thousand is deferred revenue expenditure, because its benefit lasts three years.

slides.heading: Why the distinction matters

rows: A capital item is charged as an expense
A revenue item is added to an asset

visual.alt: Table of the effect on profit and on the asset when a capital item is charged as an expense, when a revenue item is added to an asset, and when both are treated correctly

slides.narration: The class of an item decides where it is recorded, so a wrong class misstates two things at once. If a capital item is charged as an expense, profit is understated and the asset is understated. If a revenue item is added to an asset, profit is overstated and the asset is overstated. The owner, the lenders and the tax authorities all rely on correct figures.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the effect of two wrong treatments
slides.body_md: **Sheetal Dyers**, an imagined firm, reported a profit of **₹90,000**. After correcting two items, the profit is **₹95,000**.

rows: Fitting charges of a new machine ₹8,000

visual.alt: Effect of two wrong treatments in Sheetal Dyers: fitting charges of 8,000 rupees charged to wages understate profit and the machinery; repairs of 3,000 rupees added to the building overstate profit and the building; the reported profit of 90,000 rupees becomes 95,000 rupees

slides.narration: Sheetal Dyers, an imagined firm, reported a profit of rupees ninety thousand. Fitting charges of rupees eight thousand were charged to wages, so profit was understated and the machine was understated. Repairs of rupees three thousand were added to the building, so profit was overstated and the building was overstated. The correct profit is rupees ninety five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: the cost of a machine
slides.body_md: Find the amount to be debited to the machinery account of an imagined firm.
slides.narration: Add every payment that was needed to bring the new machine to the factory and make it ready to work. Leave out anything spent on a different, old machine, because that is a repair and belongs to the expenses of the year.

slides.heading: Who reads the financial statements?

rows: The profit earned and the value of the capital
Whether interest and the loan can be repaid
Whether the firm can pay its dues on time
The strength of the business and its capacity to pay
The profit on which tax is assessed

visual.alt: Table of five stakeholders of a business and what the financial statements tell each of them: proprietor, lenders and banks, suppliers on credit, employees and tax authorities

slides.narration: Financial statements are read by many people. The proprietor looks at the profit and the capital. Lenders and banks look at whether interest and the loan can be repaid. Suppliers on credit look at whether dues will be paid on time. Employees look at the strength of the business, and the tax authorities look at the profit on which tax is assessed.

slides.heading: The Trading Account
slides.body_md: The **Trading Account** finds the **gross profit** or **gross loss** from buying and selling goods.

rows: Direct expenses: wages, carriage inwards, freight, power and fuel, import duty
Gross loss, if the debit side is larger
Gross profit, if the credit side is larger

visual.alt: Table of the items on the debit side and the credit side of the Trading Account, with the gross profit or gross loss as the balancing figure

slides.narration: The trading account is prepared to find the gross profit or gross loss. On the debit side go opening stock, purchases less returns, and direct expenses. On the credit side go sales less returns and closing stock. If the credit side is larger, the difference is the gross profit. If the debit side is larger, the difference is the gross loss.

visual.caption: Direct expenses go to the Trading Account; indirect expenses go to the Profit and Loss Account.

slides.narration: Direct expenses are the costs of buying or making the goods and bringing them to a saleable state, for example wages, carriage inwards, freight, power and fuel, and import duty. They are debited to the trading account. Indirect expenses are the office, selling and financial costs, such as salaries, rent, advertising, carriage outwards and interest. They are debited to the profit and loss account.

slides.heading: Quick check: direct or indirect?
slides.body_md: Decide where carriage on purchases is shown for an imagined hardware shop.
slides.narration: Ask whether the cost helps to get the goods ready for sale, or whether it is a running cost of the office or of selling. Carriage on goods bought is incurred to bring the goods to the godown.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the trial balance of Farhan Textiles
slides.body_md: The trial balance of **Farhan Textiles** on 31 March 2026 has twenty accounts and totals **₹14,64,000** on each side. Closing stock of **₹1,20,000** is given outside it.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Farhan Textiles on 31 March 2026: twenty accounts, the debit column and the credit column each totalling 14,64,000 rupees; closing stock of 1,20,000 rupees is given outside the trial balance

slides.narration: This is the trial balance of Farhan Textiles, an imagined firm, on the last day of March two thousand twenty six. It has twenty accounts, and each column totals rupees fourteen lakh sixty four thousand. Closing stock of rupees one lakh twenty thousand is not in the trial balance. It is given separately, because the stock was counted and valued at the end of the year.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: where each item goes
slides.body_md: Every balance of the trial balance is used **exactly once**, in the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account or the Balance Sheet.

visual.alt: Where each of the twenty trial balance items of Farhan Textiles goes: each item is used exactly once in the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account or the Balance Sheet

slides.narration: Look at the last column. Opening stock, purchases, wages and carriage inwards go to the trading account, with returns deducted from purchases and sales. Salaries, rent, advertising and commission go to the profit and loss account. Drawings, capital, the loan, creditors and the assets go to the balance sheet. Every balance is used once and only once.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the Trading Account of Farhan Textiles
slides.body_md: Net sales plus closing stock exceed the debit items, so the gross profit is **₹2,94,000**.

visual.alt: Trading Account of Farhan Textiles for the year ended 31 March 2026: debit side opening stock 90,000, net purchases 6,02,000, carriage inwards 12,000 and wages 48,000; credit side net sales 9,26,000 and closing stock 1,20,000; gross profit 2,94,000 rupees

slides.narration: Net purchases are purchases less purchases returns, which is rupees six lakh two thousand. Net sales are sales less sales returns, which is rupees nine lakh twenty six thousand. The debit side holds opening stock, net purchases, carriage inwards and wages. The credit side holds net sales and closing stock. The credit side is larger, so the gross profit is rupees two lakh ninety four thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: gross profit
slides.body_md: Find the gross profit of an imagined store from its trading figures.
slides.narration: Add net sales and closing stock on the credit side. Add opening stock, purchases and direct expenses on the debit side. The gross profit is the difference between the two sides.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Capital expenditure: benefit beyond a year, acquires or improves a fixed asset.
Revenue expenditure: used up within the year, charged to the accounts.
The Trading Account gives the gross profit or gross loss.

rows: Benefit beyond one year; acquires or improves a fixed asset; non-recurring; an asset
Benefit within the year; runs the business or maintains assets; recurring; charged to the accounts
A wrong class misstates both the profit and the asset values
Opening stock, net purchases and direct expenses against net sales and closing stock give the gross result
Direct expenses go to the Trading Account; indirect expenses go to the Profit and Loss Account

visual.alt: Summary table of capital and revenue expenditure, the importance of the distinction, the Trading Account and the direct and indirect expenses

slides.narration: To sum up. Capital expenditure gives a benefit beyond one year and acquires or improves a fixed asset. Revenue expenditure is used up within the year and is charged to the accounts. A wrong class misstates both profit and asset values. The trading account sets net sales and closing stock against opening stock, net purchases and direct expenses to find the gross profit or gross loss.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give the class and the reason for each item.
Add carriage and fitting to the cost of a new asset.
Deduct returns, and show closing stock on the credit side.

rows: Name the class and give the reason for each item
Add carriage and fitting charges to the cost of a new asset
They are a cost of getting the asset ready
Deduct returns from purchases and from sales
Put closing stock on the credit side of the Trading Account
Otherwise the gross profit is wrong

slides.narration: In this part we complete the financial statements. The profit and loss account takes the gross profit and finds the net profit. The balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes. Then we pass the closing entries that move the year's results into capital, and the opening entry that starts the next year. We use Farhan Textiles throughout, and Gauri Bakery for a loss.

slides.heading: The Profit and Loss Account
slides.body_md: The **Profit and Loss Account** finds the **net profit** or **net loss** after the indirect expenses and the other incomes.

rows: Gross loss, if any, brought down
Office and administrative expenses: salaries, rent, insurance
Other incomes: commission, interest and rent received, discount received
Selling and distribution expenses: advertising, carriage outwards
Net loss, if the debit side is larger
Financial expenses: interest on loan, discount allowed
Losses; net profit, if the credit side is larger

visual.alt: Table of the items on the debit side and the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account, with the net profit or net loss as the balancing figure

slides.narration: The profit and loss account starts with the gross profit on the credit side, together with other incomes such as commission and interest received. On the debit side go the indirect expenses, office and administrative, selling and distribution, and financial, and also losses. If the credit side is larger, the difference is the net profit. Otherwise it is a net loss.

slides.body_md: Gross profit **₹2,94,000** and commission **₹12,000** less indirect expenses **₹1,50,000** give a net profit of **₹1,56,000**.
bullets: Operating profit, an extra measure, is gross profit less operating expenses: ₹2,94,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹1,44,000.

rows: To Net Profit (transferred to Capital A/c)

slides.narration: The credit side holds the gross profit of rupees two lakh ninety four thousand and commission received of rupees twelve thousand. The debit side holds salaries, rent and advertising, which total rupees one lakh fifty thousand. The credit side is larger, so the net profit is rupees one lakh fifty six thousand. Operating profit is gross profit less operating expenses, which is rupees one lakh forty four thousand.

slides.body_md: Find the net profit of an imagined store from its gross profit, expenses and income.
slides.narration: Add the gross profit and any other income. Then subtract all the indirect expenses. What is left is the net profit, which belongs to the proprietor.

slides.heading: The Balance Sheet
slides.body_md: The **Balance Sheet** is a statement of the assets and the liabilities of the business on a date. It is not an account.

rows: Capital: opening capital plus net profit less drawings
Fixed assets: land, building, machinery, furniture
Long-term liabilities: a loan repayable after more than a year
Investments held for the long term
Current liabilities: creditors, bills payable, outstanding amounts due within a year
Current assets: closing stock, debtors, bank, cash

slides.narration: The balance sheet shows the assets and liabilities on a given date. On the liabilities side are capital, which is opening capital plus net profit less drawings, long term liabilities, and current liabilities. On the assets side are fixed assets, investments and current assets. The two totals must agree.

rows: Putting items of the same nature together under one head
Debtors, closing stock and cash at bank under current assets
Arranging the groups and the items in a definite order
Fixed assets first and cash last, or cash first and fixed assets last

slides.narration: Grouping means putting items of the same nature together under one head. Debtors, closing stock and cash at bank, for example, all go under current assets. Marshalling means arranging the groups, and the items inside them, in a definite order. There are two orders, the order of permanence and the order of liquidity.

notes.title: Financial Statements I — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Capital expenditure and revenue expenditure
sections.body_md:
**Capital expenditure** gives a benefit for more than one accounting year. It is spent to acquire a fixed asset or to improve one, so that it earns more or lasts longer. It is non-recurring and is shown as an asset in the Balance Sheet. The cost of an asset includes everything needed to bring it to its place and make it ready for use: the price, carriage, fitting charges and legal fees.

**Revenue expenditure** is used up within the accounting year, in running the business or maintaining the assets, and it recurs. It is charged to the Trading Account or the Profit and Loss Account. **Deferred revenue expenditure** is a revenue expense whose benefit lasts for several years, for example a heavy advertising campaign; the part not yet charged is carried forward.

key_terms.definition_md: Spending that gives a benefit for more than one accounting year, to acquire a fixed asset or to improve it; it is non-recurring and is shown as an asset.

sections.heading: 2. Capital and revenue receipts; why the distinction matters
sections.body_md:
A **capital receipt** is money that does not come from the normal trading of the year and that adds to capital or reduces an asset: capital brought in by the proprietor, a loan received, the sale of a fixed asset. A **revenue receipt** comes from the normal trading and the incomes of the year: sales of goods, commission, interest and rent received.

The distinction matters because it decides whether an item reaches the Profit and Loss Account or the Balance Sheet. A capital item charged as an expense understates the profit and the asset; a revenue item added to an asset overstates the profit and the asset.

key_terms.definition_md: Money received from a source other than the normal trading of the year, such as capital introduced, a loan or the sale of a fixed asset.
Money received from the normal trading and incomes of the year, such as sales, commission, interest and rent received.

sections.heading: 4. The Trading Account
sections.body_md: The **Trading Account** (horizontal format) finds the gross profit or gross loss. **Debit side:** opening stock; purchases less purchases returns; direct expenses such as wages, carriage inwards, freight, power and fuel, and import duty. **Credit side:** sales less sales returns; closing stock. If the credit side is larger the balancing figure is the **gross profit**; otherwise it is the **gross loss**. Closing stock is usually given outside the trial balance.

The goods unsold on the last day of the year, valued at cost; it is credited in the Trading Account and shown as a current asset.

sections.heading: 5. The Profit and Loss Account
sections.body_md: The **Profit and Loss Account** finds the net profit or net loss. **Debit side:** indirect expenses (office and administrative, selling and distribution, financial) and losses, and a gross loss brought down. **Credit side:** gross profit brought down and other incomes such as commission, interest and rent received, and discount received. The excess of the gross profit and other incomes over the indirect expenses; it increases the capital of the proprietor.
The excess of the indirect expenses over the gross profit and other incomes; it reduces the capital of the proprietor.
The profit from the main activity of the business: gross profit less the operating expenses, before financial expenses and non-operating incomes.

sections.heading: 6. The Balance Sheet; grouping and marshalling
sections.body_md:
The **Balance Sheet** (horizontal format) is a statement of the assets and liabilities on a date. **Liabilities side:** capital (opening capital plus net profit less drawings), long-term liabilities, current liabilities. **Assets side:** fixed assets, investments, current assets. The totals of the two sides are equal.

**Grouping** puts items of one nature under one head; **marshalling** arranges the groups in an order: the **order of permanence** (fixed assets first, cash last; capital first) or the **order of liquidity** (cash first, fixed assets last; current liabilities first). The two orders reverse each other.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement of the assets and the liabilities, including capital, of a business on a given date.
Assets expected to be turned into cash within a year or the operating cycle, such as closing stock, debtors, bank and cash.
Amounts put in securities or other holdings, usually to earn income over the long term.
Amounts owed that are repayable after more than a year, such as a long-term loan.
Amounts owed that are payable within a year or the operating cycle, such as creditors.
Putting items of the same nature together under one head in the Balance Sheet.
Arranging the groups and items of the Balance Sheet in a definite order, either of liquidity or of permanence.

sections.heading: 7. Closing entries and the opening entry
sections.body_md:
**Closing entries** (passed on the last day of the year): (1) Trading A/c Dr. To opening stock, purchases, sales returns, direct expenses; (2) Sales A/c and Purchases Returns A/c Dr. To Trading A/c; (3) Closing Stock A/c Dr. To Trading A/c; (4) Trading A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c for a gross profit (reverse for a gross loss); (5) Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To indirect expenses and losses; (6) incomes Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c; (7) Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Capital A/c for a net profit (Capital A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c for a net loss); (8) Capital A/c Dr. To Drawings A/c.

The **opening entry** on the first day of the new year debits all the assets (closing stock as Stock A/c) and credits the Capital A/c and all the liabilities, with the narration that the balances are brought forward from the Balance Sheet.

questions.stem_md: Kamal Weavers, an imagined firm, buys a loom that will serve the business for many years. The amount spent on acquiring an asset of this kind, whose benefit lasts for more than one accounting year, is called

options.text_md: revenue expenditure
capital expenditure
deferred revenue expenditure
a revenue receipt

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** capital expenditure. Spending that acquires or improves a fixed asset and gives a benefit beyond one accounting year is capital expenditure. Revenue expenditure is used up within the year, deferred revenue expenditure is a revenue item whose benefit stretches over several years, and a revenue receipt is money coming in.

questions.stem_md: Lalit Printers, an imagined press in the imagined town of Ranipur, paid ₹9,000 to fit a newly bought printing machine in the workshop so that it could start work. This payment is

options.text_md: revenue expenditure, because it is a payment for a service
revenue expenditure, because it is paid only once
deferred revenue expenditure, because the machine will last for years
capital expenditure, because it is part of the cost of bringing the machine into use

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** capital expenditure, because it is part of the cost of bringing the machine into use. Fitting charges are part of the cost of getting a fixed asset ready for use, so they are added to the cost of the machine and treated as capital expenditure. Being a payment for a service or being paid only once does not decide the class, and the cost of an asset is not a deferred revenue item.

questions.stem_md: Rekha Tailors, an imagined shop, paid ₹3,500 during the year to repair its sewing machine so that it could keep running at its usual speed. In the books this is

options.text_md: revenue expenditure, charged to the Profit and Loss Account
capital expenditure, added to the cost of the machine
a capital loss, shown in the Balance Sheet
deferred revenue expenditure, spread over later years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** revenue expenditure, charged to the Profit and Loss Account. A repair that only maintains the machine in its existing condition gives a benefit within the year, so it is revenue expenditure and is charged to the Profit and Loss Account. Adding it to the machine would overstate the asset, and nothing in the payment improves the machine or spreads its benefit over later years.

questions.stem_md: Sunita Mills, an imagined firm, spent ₹60,000 on replacing the motor of its old spinning machine with a better one, which raises the machine's output by a third and lengthens its working life by four years. The expenditure is

options.text_md: revenue expenditure, because a motor is a small part of the machine
revenue expenditure, because it is a repair
capital expenditure, because it improves a fixed asset
a deferred revenue expenditure, because it covers four years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** capital expenditure, because it improves a fixed asset. Spending that increases the capacity or the life of a fixed asset is capital expenditure, whatever the size of the part replaced. It is not a repair that merely maintains the machine, and a deferred revenue item is an expense such as heavy advertising, not an improvement to an asset.

questions.stem_md: Tarun Fabrics, an imagined firm, sold an old delivery van that it no longer needed and received ₹85,000 in cash. This amount is

options.text_md: a revenue receipt
revenue expenditure
a capital receipt
drawings of the proprietor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a capital receipt. The van is a fixed asset, so money from selling it is a capital receipt. Revenue receipts arise from the normal sale of goods and services and from incomes such as commission, and the proprietor taking money out is a different matter, drawings.

questions.stem_md: Vimal Footwear, an imagined firm, spent ₹1,20,000 on a heavy advertising campaign to launch a new range, and expects the benefit to last for about three years. Such an expense is best described as

options.text_md: deferred revenue expenditure
capital expenditure
an ordinary revenue receipt
a drawing by the proprietor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** deferred revenue expenditure. A revenue expense whose benefit is expected to last beyond the year in which it is incurred is deferred revenue expenditure, and the part not yet written off is carried forward. It does not create a fixed asset, so it is not capital expenditure.

questions.stem_md: Anita Looms, an imagined firm, paid ₹9,000 as fitting charges on a new machine and debited the amount to Wages A/c. As a result, for the year,

options.text_md: profit is overstated and the machine is shown at too low a value
profit is understated and the machine is shown at too high a value
profit and the machine are both correctly stated
profit is understated and the machine is shown at too low a value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** profit is understated and the machine is shown at too low a value. The fitting charges are capital and belong in the cost of the machine. Charging them to wages makes the expenses too high, so profit is too low, and leaves the machine without the fitting charges, so the asset is too low.

questions.stem_md: Bharat Cycles, an imagined shop, spent ₹5,000 on repainting the walls of its showroom and debited the amount to Building A/c. The effect is that

options.text_md: profit is understated and the building is shown at too high a value
profit is overstated and the building is shown at too high a value
profit is overstated and the building is shown at too low a value
profit is understated and the building is shown at too low a value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** profit is overstated and the building is shown at too high a value. Repainting maintains the building and is a revenue expense. Debiting it to the building leaves the expenses too low, so profit is too high, and makes the building appear worth more than it is.

questions.stem_md: A bank is deciding whether to lend money to Tarun Plastics, an imagined firm. From the financial statements of the firm it is mainly interested in

options.text_md: the firm's ability to pay interest and repay the loan
the amount of drawings the proprietor has taken
the opening stock of the firm
the rate at which the firm pays its workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the firm's ability to pay interest and repay the loan. A lender wants to judge whether the business can pay interest and repay the principal, which the Balance Sheet and the profit shown by the statements indicate. The other items matter to the proprietor or to the staff rather than to the bank.

questions.stem_md: For a trader, the credit side of the Trading Account at the end of the year contains

options.text_md: opening stock and purchases
net sales and closing stock
direct expenses and gross loss
indirect expenses and net profit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** net sales and closing stock. Sales less returns and closing stock are credited, and opening stock, purchases and direct expenses are debited. Indirect expenses and the net profit belong to the Profit and Loss Account, and gross loss appears on the credit side only when the debit side is larger.

questions.stem_md: Nitin Hardware, an imagined shop, paid ₹12,000 to bring the goods it bought to its godown. This carriage on purchases is

options.text_md: an indirect expense, shown on the debit side of the Profit and Loss Account
a capital expenditure, shown in the Balance Sheet
a direct expense, shown on the debit side of the Trading Account
an income, shown on the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a direct expense, shown on the debit side of the Trading Account. Carriage on purchases is part of the cost of getting the goods ready for sale, so it is a direct expense in the Trading Account. Indirect expenses are the office, selling and financial costs, and carriage on goods bought does not create an asset or earn income.

questions.stem_md: Charu Sports, an imagined firm, pays the carriage on goods it sends to its customers. At the end of the year this carriage outwards is

options.text_md: debited to the Trading Account as a direct expense
credited to the Profit and Loss Account as an income
shown as an asset in the Balance Sheet
debited to the Profit and Loss Account as a selling and distribution expense

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debited to the Profit and Loss Account as a selling and distribution expense. Carriage on goods sent out is a selling and distribution cost, an indirect expense, and goes to the Profit and Loss Account. It is not part of the cost of acquiring or making the goods, so it is not a Trading Account item.

questions.stem_md: Pooja Stores, an imagined shop, shows these figures for the year ended 31 March 2026: opening stock ₹30,000, purchases ₹2,10,000, purchases returns ₹10,000, wages ₹15,000, carriage inwards ₹5,000, sales ₹3,20,000, sales returns ₹20,000 and closing stock ₹40,000. Its gross profit is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹90,000. Net sales 3,00,000 plus closing stock 40,000 less opening stock 30,000, net purchases 2,00,000 and direct expenses 20,000 gives ₹90,000. ₹1,00,000 ignores the two returns, ₹50,000 leaves out the closing stock, and ₹1,30,000 adds the direct expenses instead of deducting them.

questions.stem_md: Kavita Provisions, an imagined store, has a gross profit for the year. In its Profit and Loss Account the gross profit is shown

options.text_md: on the debit side, as the first item
on the debit side, as a deduction from indirect expenses
on the credit side, as the first item
in the Balance Sheet, on the assets side

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** on the credit side, as the first item. Gross profit is brought down from the Trading Account and credited to the Profit and Loss Account, where it is the starting income against which the indirect expenses are set. It is not an asset, and a debit would be correct only for a gross loss.

questions.stem_md: The Trading Account of Ila Garments, an imagined firm, for the year ended 31 March 2026 shows that the credit side total before the balancing figure is lower than the debit side total, a gap of ₹15,000. In its Profit and Loss Account this amount appears

options.text_md: as gross profit on the credit side
as gross loss on the debit side
as gross loss on the credit side
as net loss on the credit side

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** as gross loss on the debit side. A gross loss is an expense that has to be met out of the other incomes, so it is brought down to the debit side of the Profit and Loss Account. A credit entry would show it as a profit, and the net loss is found only after all the other items have been entered.

questions.stem_md: Rahul Cycles, an imagined firm, began the year with capital of ₹2,50,000, earned a net profit of ₹70,000 and had drawings of ₹40,000. In its Balance Sheet at the end of the year, the capital is shown as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹2,80,000. Closing capital is opening capital plus net profit less drawings, 2,50,000 + 70,000 − 40,000 = ₹2,80,000. ₹3,20,000 forgets the drawings, ₹3,60,000 adds them instead of deducting them, and ₹2,20,000 reverses both adjustments.

questions.stem_md: Aman Traders, an imagined firm, shows its Balance Sheet in the order of permanence. The first item on the assets side is then

options.text_md: cash in hand
land and building
debtors
closing stock

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** land and building. In the order of permanence the most permanent asset comes first, so fixed assets such as land and building lead and cash comes last. Cash in hand is the first item only in the order of liquidity, and debtors and stock are current assets that follow the fixed assets.

questions.stem_md: Deepak Electronics, an imagined shop, arranges its Balance Sheet in the order of liquidity. On the assets side the items then run from

options.text_md: the least easily turned into cash to the most easily turned into cash
the largest amount to the smallest amount
the oldest asset to the newest asset
the most easily turned into cash to the least easily turned into cash

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the most easily turned into cash to the least easily turned into cash. The order of liquidity puts cash first and ends with the fixed assets that are hardest to turn into cash. The reverse describes the order of permanence, and neither order depends on the size or age of the item.

questions.stem_md: Zeenat Garments, an imagined firm, arranges the headings of its Balance Sheet, such as fixed assets, investments and current assets, in a fixed sequence in either the order of liquidity or the order of permanence. This arrangement is called

options.text_md: marshalling
grouping
balancing
posting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** marshalling. Marshalling is the arrangement of the groups of assets and liabilities in a definite order. Grouping is putting like items under one head, balancing is finding the difference of two sides of an account, and posting is copying journal entries into the ledger.

questions.stem_md: Kunal Traders, an imagined firm, shows in its trial balance Debtors ₹45,000, Furniture ₹30,000, Bank Loan ₹1,00,000 repayable after five years and Creditors ₹25,000. Which item is grouped under current liabilities in its Balance Sheet?

options.text_md: Bank Loan
Debtors
Creditors
Furniture

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Creditors. Creditors are amounts due within the normal operating cycle, so they are a current liability. The bank loan repayable after five years is a long-term liability, and debtors and furniture are assets, current and fixed respectively.

questions.stem_md: At the end of the year Dinesh Stores, an imagined shop, passes a closing entry to transfer its opening stock and purchases so that the gross profit can be found. The account debited is

options.text_md: Profit and Loss Account
Capital Account
Trading Account
Drawings Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Trading Account. Opening stock and purchases are credited in their own accounts to close them, and the amount is debited to the Trading Account, where the gross profit is found. The Profit and Loss Account takes the indirect items, and capital and drawings come last.

questions.stem_md: Mohan Mobiles, an imagined shop, finds a net profit of ₹84,000 for the year. The closing entry that transfers it is

options.text_md: Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹84,000 To Capital A/c
Capital A/c Dr. ₹84,000 To Profit and Loss A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹84,000 To Drawings A/c
Trading A/c Dr. ₹84,000 To Capital A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹84,000 To Capital A/c. The profit is closed out of the Profit and Loss Account by debiting it, and credited to the proprietor's Capital Account because profit increases capital. The reverse entry would be for a loss, and neither drawings nor the Trading Account is involved in this transfer.

questions.stem_md: Padma Books, an imagined shop, has Drawings A/c showing a debit balance of ₹36,000 on 31 March 2026. The closing entry for drawings is

options.text_md: Drawings A/c Dr. ₹36,000 To Capital A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹36,000 To Drawings A/c
Drawings A/c Dr. ₹36,000 To Profit and Loss A/c
Capital A/c Dr. ₹36,000 To Drawings A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Capital A/c Dr. ₹36,000 To Drawings A/c. Drawings reduce the capital of the proprietor, so the Capital Account is debited and the Drawings Account, which carries a debit balance, is credited to close it. Drawings are not an expense of the business, so the Profit and Loss Account is not involved.

questions.stem_md: The Balance Sheet of Sonal Stores, an imagined firm, on 31 March 2026 shows capital ₹2,10,000, creditors ₹40,000, machinery ₹1,50,000 and stock, debtors and cash together ₹1,00,000. The opening entry on 1 April 2026

options.text_md: debits the creditors and the Capital Account and credits the assets
debits the assets and credits the creditors and the Capital Account
debits the Capital Account and credits all other accounts
debits the Balance Sheet and credits the Trading Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** debits the assets and credits the creditors and the Capital Account. The opening entry re-opens the books by debiting every asset and crediting every liability and the capital, so that each account carries its balance forward. The other options reverse this or bring in accounts that are not part of the Balance Sheet.

questions.stem_md: Sagar Garments, an imagined firm, has closing stock of ₹64,000 on 31 March 2026 that is not in its trial balance. The closing entry that brings it into the books is

questions.solution_md: Four points of difference with two examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Capital expenditure gives a benefit for more than one year, whereas revenue expenditure is used up within the year. Capital expenditure is incurred to acquire or improve a fixed asset, whereas revenue expenditure is incurred to run the business or to maintain assets. Capital expenditure is non-recurring, whereas revenue expenditure recurs. Capital expenditure appears as an asset in the Balance Sheet, whereas revenue expenditure is charged to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account. Examples of capital expenditure: purchase of a furnace, cost of installing it. Examples of revenue expenditure: wages, repairs to the furnace.
